title: Real-time Gen API sandbox setup — stream control, throttling & retry playbook
next_steps: Set up performance POC run next week
action_items: Maya Patel: Share sandbox credentials and quickstart notebook (due: 2027-01-05)
Luca Chen: Draft POC test plan + synthetic workload script (due: 2027-01-08)
Tom Alvarez: Confirm internal compliance checklist items for POC (due: 2027-01-03)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-29 16:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (Redwood SE), Sara (Brightline Product), Tom (Brightline Staff Eng), Elena (Brightline Sec)
Notes: sandbox-focused demo: streaming behavior, throttling/backpressure, retry semantics, SLOs and console monitor.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, um this is maya from redwood, i'm the AE on your account, and with me is luca, our systems SE. how's the audio?
[00:18] Sara: good, yeah can hear you, thanks. excited to get the sandbox spun up.
[00:25] Luca: awesome. quick agenda: we'll handoff the sandbox access, do a short live demo of real-time chat generation, show streaming chunks and controls, then go into throttling & retry patterns and how the console + optimize tab helps tune cost vs latency.
[00:40] Tom: that's perfect, we want to validate latency under our bursty load and understand what happens when we hit limits.
[00:49] Elena: also need to double-check data retention and KMS integration before any POC data goes in.

[01:05] Luca: totally. on the security front redwood private options support customer-owned KMS and retention policies, but for this sandbox we give ephemeral keys; we'll share the security sheet after.
[01:20] Maya: (links) -- sandbox creds: https://redwood.example/sandbox/BRIGHTLINE and quickstart notebook: https://redwood.example/quickstarts/sandbox-llm.ipynb

[01:42] Sara: nice, ok show us the streaming behavior you mentioned.
[01:48] Luca: sure. starting with a simple chat request. two knobs most teams use: streaming chunk size (streamed delta tokens) and early partial flush interval — basically how often we push partial tokens to the client. in our SDK it's set to 200ms by default, you can tune that to reduce latency at the cost of more-ish network chattiness.
[02:20] Maya: one thing customers confuse is streaming "granularity" vs token batching. granularity controls when bytes arrive to the client. batching controls how the runtime groups requests on the GPU to improve throughput.
[02:38] Tom: so batching is behind the scenes, and streaming is client-side?
[02:43] Luca: yep, batching is automatic in the serving runtime. it groups concurrent requests that are compatible (same model family, similar sequence length) to amortize kernel overhead. streaming flushes partial outputs immediately after generation steps.
[02:58] Sara: if we have a UI that expects immediate char-by-char updates, does that force us to lose batching?
[03:05] Luca: not necessarily. the runtime does continuous batching at the token level. small outputs still get batched as they come in, but if you require very low flush latency you may see slightly less batching efficiency. That's where the Optimize tab helps: it suggests an effective flush interval and batch window based on your traffic profile.

[03:35] [demo starts, screen-share audio noise]
[03:39] Luca: i'm sending a prompt that asks for a short chat reply, you'll see the stream come in chunks, and i'll toggle the flush interval to show the impact.
[03:52] [04:00] Sara: yeah i'm seeing it — initial token at ~80ms then chunks at ~220ms. looks good.
[04:15] Luca: great. next piece: throttling. there are two places you can experience throttling: client-side concurrency limits (our API enforces per-key concurrency) and server-side capacity signals which return 429 or a 503 depending on overload.
[04:35] Maya: and we also have a concept of rate-limit buckets by route, so embeddings vs chat might have separate quotas.
[04:44] Tom: what's our recommendation for handling 429s? exponential backoff?
[04:49] Luca: yes, backoff + jitter for 429s is typical. we recommend using idempotency keys for non-chat generate requests when you might retry to avoid double billing or duplicate actions. for streaming sessions we'd re-establish the stream with the conversation_id and message_id so you can continue from the last committed step.
[05:10] Sara: how do you recommend we detect a partial streaming failure vs a full session termination?
[05:16] Luca: good question. the client SDK exposes connection events: partial-close vs final-err. we log a token-offset checkpoint periodically (the KV cache offset), so on reconnect you can request to continue from offset N. transcription sometimes shows that as "K V cash offset" which is the KV cache; sorry the ASR likes to mangle that.
[05:39] Elena: (laughs) noted. on the security side, if we reconnect does anything persist in your logs? we need to know retention and redaction.
[05:48] Maya: sandbox logs are ephemeral and redacted; for production you can set retention policy and enable encryption-at-rest with your KMS. we'll attach the SOC2/ISO sheet.

[06:00] Luca: now let's simulate hitting concurrency caps. i'll open multiple simultaneous streams — note the per-key concurrency default for hosted is 50 concurrent streams, you can request higher or move to dedicated for guaranteed capacity.
[06:18] [06:30] Tom: ok i see 1-2x latency bump when you cross 50. we'll want to know how that curve looks at 200-500 concurrent sessions.
[06:41] Luca: for those volumes we usually recommend a POC on dedicated or a large reserved pool; or elastic burst with dedicated + hosted fallback. Redwood's routing can fallback to a cheaper quantized variant if latency budget is tight.
[06:58] Sara: fallback — is that automatic? do we control policy?
[07:02] Maya: you control policy in the console rollout rules. typical policy is: prefer primary model, fallback to quantized model on high p95 latency or explicit capacity shortage. you can set region-based fallbacks too.
[07:16] Elena: what's the visibility during a fallback? can we see which model served each request?
[07:20] Luca: yes — the request-level trace includes model_id, kernel_variant, and latency breakdown. console traces and the per-token cost are shown.

[07:40] [07:55] Luca: retry patterns — short summary: on 429 -> retry with exponential backoff + jitter; on 5xx -> small number of retries, and if you see repeated 5xx escalate to fallback model or circuit-breaker. also respect Retry-After header where present.
[08:10] Tom: how about idempotency and exactly-once for streaming?
[08:15] Luca: for streaming, we recommend app-level dedupe with message IDs: client sends message_id, server writes checkpoint, if reconnect happens you pass last_committed_id. for non-streaming generates use an idempotency token.

[08:35] Sara: curious about cost — how do retries impact billing?
[08:39] Maya: billing is per token served. partial retries that re-generate tokens will increase token counts, so aggressive retries can inflate cost. Optimize suggests safe retry budgets and lets you simulate cost for given retry policies.
[08:55] Luca: also quantized model variants reduce per-token cost and are good fallback to preserve availability. the console Optimize tab gives a delta: estimated latency vs unit cost for each variant.

[09:15] [09:30] Demo: console Optimize view — Luca toggles suggestions
[09:36] Luca: here's an Optimize recommendation: increase max_batch_window from 20ms to 60ms for this workload — it increases throughput by 18% while p95 latency only increases 30ms.
[09:48] Tom: we'd need the p95 number — can you show the historical p95 in the monitoring panel?
[09:53] Luca: yep, top-right shows p50/p95/p99. for your demo traffic p95 is 220ms currently, p50 80ms.
[10:05] Sara: ok that helps. if we accept the Optimize suggestion, will it be a gradual rollout?
[10:10] Maya: yes — canary rollout is first-class. you pick a percentage, monitor SLOs and then ramp. the console also supports automatic rollback on SLO regressions.

[10:30] [11:00] Tom: in terms of instrumentation, what traces do we need to add in our app to measure true end-to-end latency?
[11:08] Luca: stamp client-side send time, server-receive, first-byte, and last-byte. Redwood traces will populate server timings; join them with client logs via request_id. we also expose token-level timestamps in the logs for deep analysis.

[11:45] Maya: quick note about network backpressure: if your front-end uses HTTP/1.1 long polling it behaves differently than a websocket stream. websockets preserve partial flush semantics better for char-by-char UX.
[12:05] Sara: we were planning websockets. is there a recommended client library?
[12:09] Luca: our JS SDK has a websocket helper that manages reconnects and checkpoints. we'll include that in the notebook.

[12:35] [13:00] Sample edge-case talk-through: user types rapidly and issues many parallel system messages — how to protect model quality?
[13:10] Luca: enforce per-user request queues and a server-side token budget per conversation. Redwood supports token quotas per conversation to prevent runaway cost from long histories. you can evict older messages or summarize them automatically to stay within the budget.
[13:28] Tom: can the runtime do auto-summarize?
[13:31] Luca: we have optional summarization hooks in the platform; you can configure a pipeline to compress history periodically. Optimize will flag long-context usage.

[13:50] [14:10] Discussion: POC sizing and metrics
[14:15] Sara: for POC, we care about p95 latency <300ms for chat and cost per 1k tokens under $0.30. can you show how we track those?
[14:24] Maya: yes, console has custom metric dashboards; we can create a POC dashboard with those two metrics and an alert.
[14:32] Luca: also we'll run a controlled synthetic workload: 100 prov hits at steady 5 rps per user to measure steady-state, and spike tests to measure cold-burst behavior.

[15:00] [15:20] Quick aside about model version pinning and rollouts
[15:24] Maya: important to pin model versions in prod and use canary for changes. rollouts can be done across model versions or kernel variants.
[15:34] Elena: for compliance, will we get audit logs with who changed the rollout?
[15:38] Luca: yes audit logs include who, what, when, and the delta. they ship to your SIEM via syslog or S3.

[16:00] [16:30] Fault-mode scenario: large model OOMs under long context
[16:35] Luca: in long-context OOMs the runtime will surface a specific 5xx with an OOM hint; policy usually is to retry against a quantized model or reduce chunk size. we've also built kernel selection to favor memory-efficient kernels for long contexts.
[16:55] Tom: will the console flag an increase in OOMs?
[16:58] Luca: yes, there's an error-rate by type graph. Optimize can recommend switching to a memory-optimized kernel.

[17:25] [17:40] Replay of our sample reconnect flow — Luca simulates a dropped socket and recovers from KV offset
[18:05] Sara: ok we saw the continuation pick up at offset 124. good.

[18:20] Maya: moving into retry budget policies — many customers set a per-minute retry budget per conversation to prevent infinite retry storms which amplify cost. e.g., max 3 retries per message within 60s.
[18:37] Tom: makes sense, we'll adopt that.

[19:00] [19:30] Conversation about instrumentation for billing reconciliation
[19:35] Maya: attach request_id and conversation_id to each request, keep server request logs for reconciliation. we'll share a billing reconciliation template.
[19:50] Sara: great. also can we sample token payloads for QA?
[19:56] Elena: we only allow sampling with PII redaction — how does redwood handle that?
[20:03] Luca: we have a selector to redact PII in-flight and on logs; for enterprise you'll enable required redaction rules. we'll share the redact config.

[20:30] [21:00] Final POC logistics
[21:05] Maya: proposed POC timeline: week 0: sandbox and quickstart, week 1: synthetic throughput runs, week 2: integration with front-end and security sign-off, week 3: customer validates against SLOs.
[21:20] Tom: who owns the workload runner?
[21:23] Luca: we'll provide a starter JMeter script and a node-based runner; luca will own that artifact and help run the first test.

[22:00] [22:20] Sara: one more question on failover — if a region becomes unhealthy, will routing automatically failover to another region?
[22:27] Maya: yes if you enabled multi-region routing. you can prefer region A but allow failover to region B; data residency options determine whether fallbacks are allowed across regions.

[22:50] [23:10] Quick live: show cost breakdown per token in console
[23:20] Luca: here you can see per-route unit cost, and a breakdown by kernel/quantization. for example the quantized gpt-q variant is ~0.45x cost of the full FP model.

[24:00] [24:30] Sara: is there an API to pull those cost metrics?
[24:34] Maya: yes billing API exports per-request token counts to your billing export.

[25:00] [25:30] Short troubleshooting: unexpected 502s from CDN layer
[25:35] Luca: check edge timeouts first; long-running streams must be proxied with streaming-aware timeouts. our recommended edge (nginx/lb) config is in the quickstart. we'll paste it to the shared drive.

[26:10] [26:40] Question: what do you do for slow-token generation affecting perceived latency?
[26:45] Luca: some slow token generation is model-architecture dependent; Optimize will recommend kernel variants and sometimes a smaller context window or summarization. you can also do partial pre-writes for templated responses.

[27:10] [27:35] Elena: what about audit for who ran what tests?
[27:38] Luca: the audit logs include test-run metadata if you attach job_id in the request.

[28:00] [28:30] Recap and explicit next steps
[28:35] Maya: recap — we'll send sandbox creds + quickstart notebook, luca will share the starter workload and POC plan, and we'll schedule the perf run for next week. elena will send minimal compliance checklist items.
[28:52] Tom: can we get a security SLA summary?
[28:55] Maya: yes we'll attach the SOC2 summary and KMS integration doc.

[29:10] Sara: timeline sounds good. anything else on retries?
[29:14] Luca: one more note: instrument Retry-After headers and treat 429s as signals rather than transient errors. add jitter to avoid thundering herds.

[29:35] [30:00] Closing notes
[30:05] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts. expect sandbox creds and quickstart by tomorrow morning. luca will reach out to coordinate the perf window.
[30:20] Sara: appreciate it, thanks.
[30:24] Tom: thanks, bye.
[30:26] Elena: bye.

[30:40] Post-call: quick internal note by Maya: attach links to docs and secure the sandbox creds.

(Transcript ends — many timestamps skipped for brevity; audio ~48 minutes with Q&A and live demo sections. Some names and product terms may be slightly garbled by ASR: e.g., "K V cash" -> KV cache, "S S O" -> SSO.)
